text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- A record number of rental properties are standing empty in smaller towns around Sweden. The public housing sector also has never before experienced so many vacant properties even though the number of total properties on the market fell by 15,000 last year.

- Over 600 international guests have arrived in Stockholm for the funeral of Prince Bertil, who died eight days ago, aged 84. The funeral will be held at midday followed by a funeral procession to the royal graveyard just outside the city.

- Sweden is the worst country in Europe for combatting crimes against nature. Sweden has two conventions aimed at protecting the eradication of animals and plants but still has no power to enforce these laws.

- In two years time, pilots, air-traffic controllers, airplane technicians and other aircraft maintanence staff must agree to urine drug tests, according to new EU regulations. For years, Scandinavian Airlines staff has refused drug testing and particularly among SAS staff in Norway and Denmark there is strong sentiment against testing.
- Television network TV3 aims to become Sweden's largest entertainment channel, its president Casten Almqvist told the newspaper in an interview.

- Banking group S-E-Banken has 15,000 customers doing transactions via the internet, according to the bank's internet project leader Anders Lindqvist. Swedish banks have recently started offering their customers service via the net and S-E-Banken is ahead of the others in this respect.

- The payment of about 36 billion crowns to Swedish savers this year from private bonds sold in 1992 and 1994 is expected to create a scramble for the funds. The big question is whether small savers will reinvest this money in private bonds or look at investing in shares.

- Unease in Japan can provide a golden opportunity, according to Anders Lannebo, head of Sweden's biggest fund company Robur who is expecting a strong bourse in 1997. Robur expects fund savings to expand this year and the aim is for Robur in the next five years to double the funds it manages to 180 billion crown.
